title: Ζεὺς καὶ αἰσχύνη
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 118 (= Perry 109). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ζεὺς πλάσας τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τὰς μὲν ἄλλας διαθέσεις αὐτοῖς ἐνέθηκε, μόνην δ’ ἐνθεῖναι τὴν αἰσχύνην ἐπελάθετο.
sentences.tr: Zeus plasas tous anthrōpous tas men allas diatheseis autois enethēke, monēn d’ entheinai tēn aischynēn epelatheto.
sentences.l: Zeus, having moulded men, put the other dispositions into them, but forgot to put in shame alone.
sentences.i: When Zeus had moulded mankind, he put all the other dispositions into them, but shame was the one thing he forgot to put in.
sentences.n: πλάσσω is the potter's word, of shaping figures out of clay — the standard Greek picture of the making of men. διάθεσις is the settled condition of a character, the temper a person is made with. αἰσχύνη here is shame as a restraint, the sense of disgrace that holds a person back — the work more usually done by αἰδώς — rather than the feeling that follows a fault.

sentences.t: Διὸ καὶ μὴ ἔχων πόθεν [ἂν] αὐτὴν εἰσαγάγῃ, διὰ τοῦ ἀρχοῦ αὐτὴν εἰσελθεῖν ἐκέλευσεν.
sentences.tr: Dio kai mē echōn pothen [an] autēn eisagagēi, dia tou archou autēn eiselthein ekeleusen.
sentences.l: And so, having nowhere from which he [might] bring her in, he ordered her to enter through the fundament.
sentences.i: So, having no way to bring her in, he told her to go in by the fundament.
sentences.n: The square brackets are Chambry's: he prints ἄν but judges it interpolated and marks it for deletion, so the brackets in the literal line cover just that word. Without it the clause is a plain deliberative subjunctive in an indirect question — 'having no answer to the question, from where am I to bring her in?'. ἀρχός is the anatomical term for the rectum; the fable is a coarse joke and its last line depends on the word, so it is not softened here.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ἀντέλεγεν ἀναξιοπαθοῦσα.
sentences.tr: Hē de to men prōton antelegen anaxiopathousa.
sentences.l: But she at first spoke against it, feeling herself unworthily used.
sentences.n: ἀναξιοπαθέω is a single verb for the whole idea: to suffer what one does not deserve, and to resent it. τὸ πρῶτον is adverbial accusative, 'at first' — and implies, as it usually does, that she did not hold out.

sentences.t: Ἐπεὶ δὲ σφόδρα αὐτῇ ἐνέκειτο, ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε ἐπὶ ταύταις εἰσέρχομαι ταῖς ὁμολογίαις ὡς Ἔρως μὴ εἰσελεύσεται· ἂν δ’ εἰσέλθη, αὐτὴ ἐξελεύσομαι παραυτίκα. »
sentences.tr: Epei de sphodra autēi enekeito, ephē· « All’ egōge epi tautais eiserchomai tais homologiais hōs Erōs mē eiseleusetai· an d’ eiselthē, autē exeleusomai parautika. »
sentences.l: And when he pressed hard upon her, she said: « Well, I for my part go in on these terms, that Eros shall not come in; and if he does come in, I myself will go straight out. »
sentences.n: ἔγκειμαι with the dative is to lie on top of someone, hence to press and insist. ἐπὶ ταύταις ταῖς ὁμολογίαις is ἐπί with the dative of the terms on which a thing is done, and ὡς with the future indicative gives the content of the compact. The page reads εἰσέλθη, without the iota subscript the subjunctive εἰσέλθῃ would carry; it is left as printed rather than corrected. Ἔρως is Desire personified, as αἰσχύνη is throughout this fable — the two cannot occupy the same person.

sentences.t: Ἀπὸ δὴ τούτου συνέβη πάντας τοὺς πόρνους ἀναισχύντους εἶναι.
sentences.tr: Apo dē toutou synebē pantas tous pornous anaischyntous einai.
sentences.l: From this indeed it came about that all men who sell themselves are without shame.
sentences.n: πόρνος is the masculine of πόρνη: a man who sells himself. The fable derives the fact from its anatomy joke, Shame having entered by the way she did and left as soon as Desire arrived. συνέβη takes the accusative and infinitive, 'it came about that…'.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι τοὺς ὑπ’ Ἔρωτος κατεχομένους ἀναισχύντους εἶναι συμβαίνει.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti tous hyp’ Erōtos katechomenous anaischyntous einai symbainei.
sentences.l: The fable shows that it comes about that those held fast by Eros are without shame.
sentences.i: The fable shows that those held in the grip of Eros turn out to be shameless.
sentences.n: κατέχομαι with ὑπό and the genitive is the language of possession by a god or a passion — held down, not merely influenced. The moral widens the tale from the πόρνοι of the last line to anyone Eros has taken hold of.
